question.problem:
Sarah conducts an experiment $40$ times to see how quickly a machine sorts a bin of parts. The table below shows the results of her experiments.

| Time (seconds) | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| $<20$ | $6$ |
| $20-30$ | $16$ |
| $30-40$ | $10$ |
| $40-50$ | $5$ |
| $>50$ | $3$ |

Based on the experimental probabilities of these results, complete the following statements.

$\,$A machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds is
{{field-1}}.

$\,$A machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds is
{{field-2}}.

$\,$A machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds is
{{field-3}}
a machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds.
question.worked_solution:
One event is more likely than another if it has a greater probability of occurring. If two events have the same probability, they are equally likely.

Let's consider each statement in turn.

- To compute the experimental probability of a machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds, we divide the number of times a machine sorted a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds $(6+16=22)$ by the total number of times Sarah conducted the experiment $(40).$ This gives

$$
P(\text{sorts in }<30\text{ seconds})=\frac{22}{40}.
$$

This probability is a relatively large number, closer to $1.$ Since

$$
\frac{1}{2}<\frac{22}{40}<1,
$$

this event is $\text{likely}.$

- To compute the experimental probability of a machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds, we divide the number of times a machine sorted a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds $(10+5+3=18)$ by the total number of times Sarah conducted the experiment $(40).$ This gives

$$
P(\text{sorts in }>30\text{ seconds})=\frac{18}{40}.
$$

This probability is a small number, closer to $0.$ Since

$$
0<\frac{18}{40}<\frac{1}{2},
$$

this event is $\text{unlikely}.$

- The experimental probability of a machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds is *greater than* the experimental probability of a machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds:

$$
P(\text{sorts in }<30\text{ seconds})=\frac{22}{40}>\frac{18}{40}=P(\text{sorts in }>30\text{ seconds})
$$

Therefore, a machine sorting a bin of parts in less than $30$ seconds is
$\text{more likely than}$
a machine sorting a bin of parts in more than $30$ seconds.
